steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a security paper on how commercial LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, Bard) can be misused to generate phishing websites and emails, and on our machine-learning model for detecting such malicious prompts early. Cover the motivation, how the paper is organized section by section, and a list of contributions.

- Phishing kits and LLMs as a new alternative
- Our goals and the structure of the paper (Sections II-VII)
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years Large Language Models (LLMs) have brought a transformative era in natural language processing, since they can easily generate responses that closely emulate human-like conversation on a more and more diverse range of subjects. LLMs have also been used for many applications, for example content creation for marketing, troubleshooting in software development, and providing resources for digital learning. The vast utility of LLMs has also got the attention of malicious actors who want to exploit them for social engineering scams, including phishing attacks. These models are designed with safeguards that identify and reject prompts that may be harmful or misleading, but attackers can skillfully get around these protections. This has led to malevolent content being generated, including deceptive emails, fraudulent investment and romantic schemes, and even malware creations. Also, underground hacker forums are full of discussions about manipulating LLMs for more advanced malicious purposes, which further encourages newer attackers to adopt LLMs.

Open-source LLMs can be modified to produce malicious content, but deploying local models needs significant hardware, time, and technical expertise. Commercially available LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Bard on the other hand are readily accessible to the public at no cost. They are more convenient to access, and they are also backed by superior architectures that are proprietary and/or too resource-intensive for one person to run locally at scale. Because these powerful models are so easy to get, attackers are motivated to abuse them for social engineering scams such as phishing attacks. Once phishing attacks are created they are spread widely through several online channels, and email is the most common one. Attackers write emails that imitate a popular organization or a familiar personality, trying to incentivize or imitate the potential victim into clicking a website link. This link is the phishing website, and it is used to collect sensitive information from the victim (like bank details, account credentials, and Social Security numbers), which is then sent back to the attacker who can use it for nefarious purposes. The damage from phishing attacks is enormous, with reported financial losses of $52 million in the last year alone. As a countermeasure, anti-phishing measures, both commercial solutions and open-source implementations, keep trying to take these attacks down quickly. But attackers keep innovating and use different techniques to evade detection, so the attacks can stay active for a long time.

Over time knowledgable users have learned to recognize the telltale signs of fake emails and websites, such as grammatical errors and poor website design and execution. In response attackers use phishing kits, which are automated tools that craft these attacks with little or no manual work. Anti-phishing strategies often focus on identifying these kits, because detecting one kit helps find all the attacks that come from that kit. However, LLMs are an innovative alternative, using natural language processing. LLMs have already shown that they are good at generating source code in many programming languages. So attackers could potentially prompt LLMs to craft phishing websites and emails and then use this content to orchestrate and unleash their attacks.

- Goals and structure
  - goals: extent of misuse of commercial LLMs; effectiveness/functionality of generated attacks; countermeasure for early detection of malicious prompts
  - Sec II: applications of LLMs + challenges of misuse
  - Sec III: threat model
  - Sec IV: methodology (feasibility/effectiveness, ML-based detection model)
  - Sec V: phishing websites; LLMs deny overt malicious prompts -> framework of seemingly benign prompts, combined or sequential; regular + seven evasive attack vectors via manually designed prompts; recursive: LLMs generate phishing prompts, fed back -> website source code; judge appearance and functionality
  - Sec VI: phishing emails; prompts inspired by live phishing emails from APWG eCrimeX (cite); compare with text generation metrics
  - Sec VII: ML model detects malicious prompts in real time; early detection stops further prompts
- Contributions
  1. compare ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo, GPT 4, Claude, Bard for conventional + evasive phishing websites and emails; prompts evade moderation, LLMs generate malicious prompts automatically; attacks convincing and as resistant to detection as human/kit-made
  2. first dataset of malicious prompts: 1,255 phishing-related prompts (regular + seven evasive), 2,109 phishing email prompts
  3. ML model for early detection; trained on ChatGPT and GPT-4 prompts, works on Claude and Bard; avg accuracy 96% website prompts, 94% email
  4. model and codebook: https://tinyurl.com/epu6w4cp
  5. Huggingface: https://huggingface.co/phishbot/ScamLLM; ChatGPT actions plugin: https://chat.openai.com/g/g-KU1izdZTw-prompt-defender
  6. disclosed vulnerabilities to Google, Anthropic, OpenAI

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years Large Language Models (LLMs) have brought a transformative era in natural language processing, since they can easily generate responses that closely emulate human-like conversation on a more and more diverse range of subjects. LLMs have also been used for many applications, for example content creation for marketing, troubleshooting in software development, and providing resources for digital learning. The vast utility of LLMs has also got the attention of malicious actors who want to exploit them for social engineering scams, including phishing attacks. These models are designed with safeguards that identify and reject prompts that may be harmful or misleading, but attackers can skillfully get around these protections. This has led to malevolent content being generated, including deceptive emails, fraudulent investment and romantic schemes, and even malware creations. Also, underground hacker forums are full of discussions about manipulating LLMs for more advanced malicious purposes, which further encourages newer attackers to adopt LLMs.

Open-source LLMs can be modified to produce malicious content, but deploying local models needs significant hardware, time, and technical expertise. Commercially available LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Bard on the other hand are readily accessible to the public at no cost. They are more convenient to access, and they are also backed by superior architectures that are proprietary and/or too resource-intensive for one person to run locally at scale. Because these powerful models are so easy to get, attackers are motivated to abuse them for social engineering scams such as phishing attacks. Once phishing attacks are created they are spread widely through several online channels, and email is the most common one. Attackers write emails that imitate a popular organization or a familiar personality, trying to incentivize or imitate the potential victim into clicking a website link. This link is the phishing website, and it is used to collect sensitive information from the victim (like bank details, account credentials, and Social Security numbers), which is then sent back to the attacker who can use it for nefarious purposes. The damage from phishing attacks is enormous, with reported financial losses of $52 million in the last year alone. As a countermeasure, anti-phishing measures, both commercial solutions and open-source implementations, keep trying to take these attacks down quickly. But attackers keep innovating and use different techniques to evade detection, so the attacks can stay active for a long time.

Over time knowledgable users have learned to recognize the telltale signs of fake emails and websites, such as grammatical errors and poor website design and execution. In response attackers use phishing kits, which are automated tools that craft these attacks with little or no manual work. Anti-phishing strategies often focus on identifying these kits, because detecting one kit helps find all the attacks that come from that kit. However, LLMs are an innovative alternative, using natural language processing. LLMs have already shown that they are good at generating source code in many programming languages. So attackers could potentially prompt LLMs to craft phishing websites and emails and then use this content to orchestrate and unleash their attacks.

Our work aims to explore how far commercially available LLMs can be used for generating phishing attacks, to identify how effective these generated attacks are in terms of functionality, and finally to build an effective countermeasure that can help detect early the malicious prompts that can be used to generate such phishing scams. The paper is structured as follows. In Section II we look at the broad applications of LLMs and the challenges that come from their misuse for generating harmful content. In Section III we determine the general Threat Model for generating phishing attacks with commercial LLMs. Section IV introduces our methodology for identifying whether phishing scam generation with these commercial LLMs is feasible and effective, and for developing an ML-based model for early detection of such malicious prompts. In Section V we focus on generating phishing websites with these commercial LLMs. Since these tools are good at denying prompts with overt malicious intent, we created a framework that gives multiple prompt sentences that look benign, either combined into one prompt or given one after another. Together, the final output of these prompts can create phishing websites. We also test how well the LLMs generate both regular attacks and seven widely recognized evasive phishing attack vectors, using malicious prompts that we designed manually. We investigate the recursive nature of LLMs in generating phishing content, showing how they can be repurposed to create a growing array of phishing prompts. Feeding these prompts back into the LLM, in a cyclic manner, generates the source code of the phishing website. We assess how useful these automated prompts are for creating convincing phishing websites across all LLMs, and judge them on appearance and functionality.

In Section VI we discuss generating phishing emails with these LLMs. We use the same recursive approach of using LLMs to generate prompts, described above, and generate prompts inspired by live phishing emails taken from APWG eCrimeX. Similar to the phishing website analysis, we compare how proficient the LLMs are at generating phishing emails using several text generation metrics. Finally, in Section VII we design a machine learning model that can detect malicious prompts in real time, which prevents the LLMs from generating such phishing content. We mainly focus on early detection of the phishing prompts so that the LLM can stop the user from giving more prompts once phishing intention is detected.

The primary contributions of our work are:

- 1. We evaluate and compare how ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo, GPT 4, Claude, and Bard can be used to produce conventional and evasive phishing website attacks as well as phishing emails. We find that attackers can manipulate prompts, which lets them evade the content moderation mechanisms of these tools and also lets the LLMs generate malicious prompts automatically. These prompts can then be used to create phishing attacks that are visually and functionally convincing and also as resistant to anti-phishing detection as those made by humans or phishing kits.

- 2. We curate the first dataset of malicious prompts that can be used to produce phishing websites and emails with Large Language Models. It has 1,255 individual phishing-related prompts, covering regular and seven evasive phishing strategies, and 2,109 phishing email prompts.

- 3. We design a machine-learning model for early detection of phishing website and email prompts, to stop the LLM from generating malicious content. Our model is trained on ChatGPT and GPT-4 prompts and also performs well on Claude and Bard, with an average accuracy of 96% for phishing website prompt detection and 94% for phishing email detection.

- 4. Our model and codebook are available at: https://tinyurl.com/epu6w4cp.

- 5. The model can also be tested on Huggingface: https://huggingface.co/phishbot/ScamLLM, and as a ChatGPT actions plugin: https://chat.openai.com/g/g-KU1izdZTw-prompt-defender.

- 6. We have disclosed the vulnerabilities we found for generating phishing scams to Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI.

steps.text:
In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have brought a transformative era in natural language processing, as they can effortlessly generate responses that closely emulate human-like conversation across an increasingly diverse array of subjects. LLMs have also been used for various applications such as content creation for marketing [1], troubleshooting in software development [2], and providing resources for digital learning [3,4], among others. The vast utility of LLMs has also caught the attention of malicious actors who aim to exploit their capabilities for social engineering scams, including phishing attacks [5,6,7]. Although these models are designed with safeguards to identify and reject potentially harmful or misleading prompts [8,9], attackers can skillfully bypass these protective measures. This has led to the generation of malevolent content, including deceptive emails [10,11,12], fraudulent investment and romantic schemes [13], and even malware creations [14,15]. Moreover, underground hacker forums are rife with discussions about manipulating LLMs for more advanced malicious endeavors [16], further encouraging newer attackers to adopt LLMs for their purposes.

Although open-source LLMs can be modified to produce malicious content, deploying local models demands significant hardware, time, and technical expertise [17]. By contrast, commercially available LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Bard are readily accessible to the public at no cost. These models are not only more convenient to access but are also backed by superior architectures that are proprietary [18] and/or too resource-intensive for an individual to operate locally at scale. The ease and availability of these powerful models therefore motivate attackers to abuse them to create social engineering scams such as phishing attacks. Once created, phishing attacks are disseminated widely through several online channels, with email being the most common form of transmission [19]. Attackers craft emails that imitate a popular organization or familiar personality, attempting to incentivize or imitate the potential victim into clicking on a website link [20,21,22]. The link, which is the phishing website, is used to collect sensitive information (such as bank details, account credentials, and Social Security numbers) from the victim, which is then transmitted back to the attacker, who can use it for nefarious purposes [23]. The potential damage of phishing attacks is enormous, with reported financial losses of $52 million during the last year alone [24]. As a countermeasure, anti-phishing measures - both commercial solutions [25,26] and open-source implementations [27,28] - continuously strive to take these attacks down quickly [29]. However, attackers constantly innovate, employing various techniques to evade detection [29,30], which enables the attacks to remain active for a long period of time [31].

Over time, knowledgable users have learned to recognize the telltale signs of fake emails and websites, including grammatical errors and poor website design and execution [32]. In response, attackers employ phishing kits [33], automated tools that craft these malicious attacks with little to no manual intervention. Anti-phishing strategies often focus on identifying these kits, since detecting one kit helps identify all attacks that originate from it [34,35,36]. However, LLMs present an innovative alternative that leverages natural language processing. LLMs have already demonstrated prowess in generating source code across various programming languages [37,38]. Attackers could thus potentially prompt LLMs to craft phishing websites and emails and then use this content to orchestrate and unleash their attacks.

Our work aims to explore the extent to which commercially available LLMs can be leveraged for generating phishing attacks, to identify the effectiveness of these generated attacks with respect to functionality, and finally to build an effective countermeasure that can aid in the early detection of malicious prompts that can be used to generate such phishing scams. The paper is structured as follows: In Section II, we explore the broad applications of LLMs alongside the challenges posed by their misuse in generating harmful content. In Section III, we determine the general Threat Model that can be used to generate phishing attacks with commercial LLMs. This is followed by Section IV, where we introduce our methodology for identifying the feasibility and effectiveness of phishing scam generation using these commercial LLMs, as well as for developing an ML-based model for the early detection of such malicious prompts. In Section V, we focus on the generation of phishing websites using these commercial LLMs. Recognizing that these tools are adept at denying prompts with overt malicious intent, we have crafted a framework that provides multiple seemingly benign prompt sentences, either combined as a single prompt or given sequentially. Together, the final output of these prompts can result in phishing websites. We also test the capabilities of the LLMs at generating both regular and seven widely recognized evasive phishing attack vectors using manually designed malicious prompts. We investigate the recursive nature of LLMs in generating phishing content, illustrating how they can be repurposed to create an increasing array of phishing prompts. Feeding these prompts back into the LLM in a cyclic manner results in the source code of the phishing website. We assess the utility of these automated prompts in creating convincing phishing websites across all LLMs, judging them on both appearance and functionality.

We then discuss generating phishing emails using these LLMs in Section VI. Using the same recursive approach of having LLMs generate prompts, as described in the previous paragraph, we generate prompts inspired by live phishing emails sourced from APWG eCrimeX [39]. As in our analysis of phishing websites, we compare the proficiency of the LLMs in generating phishing emails using several text generation metrics. Finally, in Section VII, we design a machine learning model that can detect malicious prompts in real time, thus preventing the LLMs from generating such phishing content. We primarily focus on early detection of the phishing prompts, so that the LLM can prevent the user from providing further prompts once phishing intention is detected.

The primary contributions of our work are:

- 1. We evaluate and compare how ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo, GPT 4, Claude, and Bard can be leveraged to produce both conventional and evasive phishing website attacks, as well as phishing emails. Our investigation reveals that attackers can manipulate prompts, which not only allows them to evade the content moderation mechanisms of these tools but also enables the LLMs to generate malicious prompts automatically. These prompts can then be exploited to create phishing attacks that are not only visually and functionally convincing but also as resistant to anti-phishing detection measures as those crafted by humans or phishing kits.

- 2. We curate the first dataset of malicious prompts that can be used to produce phishing websites and emails using Large Language Models. It includes 1,255 individual phishing-related prompts, which cover regular as well as seven evasive phishing strategies, and 2,109 phishing email prompts.

- 3. We design a machine-learning model aimed at early detection of phishing website and email prompts to deter the LLM from generating malicious content. Our model, trained on ChatGPT and GPT-4 prompts, also performs well on Claude and Bard, achieving an average accuracy of 96% for phishing website prompt detection and 94% for phishing email detection.

- 4. We make our model and codebook available at: https://tinyurl.com/epu6w4cp.

- 5. Our model can also be tested on Huggingface: https://huggingface.co/phishbot/ScamLLM, as well as through a ChatGPT actions plugin: https://chat.openai.com/g/g-KU1izdZTw-prompt-defender.

- 6. We have also disclosed the identified vulnerabilities for generating phishing scams to Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI.
